entries.title: Rapper BloodHound Q50, 22, fatally shot in Fuller Park
entries.summary: <p>The Cook County medical examiner's office identified a 22-year-old man who was fatally shot Sunday morning in Fuller Park as Mikquale Cooper of Chicago.</p><p>A manager with AMF Music Group confirmed Cooper was the rap artist who performed as BloodHound Q50.</p><p>Chicago police said Cooper was in a car around 4 a.m. in the 4200 block of South Wentworth Avenue when two cars pulled up alongside and several people in both vehicles fired shots at him, according to police.</p><p>Cooper was shot in the chest and shoulder.</p><p>He was treated by Chicago Fire Department personnel and was pronounced dead at the scene, police said.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Bears' next opponent: Vikings score 29 straight points to beat Packers 39-22
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Carson Wentz has had little time to practice with Minnesota's voluminous playbook, a late arrival to the team last season who returned this year in more of a mentor role as Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy competed for the starting quarterback job in training camp.</p><p>The Vikings brought the 11th-year veteran back for emergencies like these.</p><p>Wentz came in after Murray's first-quarter concussion in his Minnesota debut and led a spirited comeback against the rival Green Bay Packers, as the Vikings scored 29 straight points to close a 39-22 victory to open the season on Sunday.</p><p>"That's why he's here," coach Kevin O'Connell said. "For him to come in and do what he did and just be part of that calming presence that allowed our team to continue playing, I can't say enough about him."</p><p>Wentz had two touchdown passes to Justin Jefferson, matching the two-time All-Pro's 2025 season total, and the pair connected on a 2-point conversion when the Vikings took their first lead at 25-22 with 6:37 remaining. Green Bay extended the drive three times with crushing defensive penalties.</p><p>"Football is a funny game," Wentz said, "but it's fun to be on this side of it."</p><p>Jordan Love, who had been brilliant against a relentlessly blitzing defense, wilted along with the rest of the team by losing a fumble on a sack and throwing an interception deep in Packers territory.</p><p>Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason each had rushing touchdowns and T.J. Hockenson caught one of the three scores thrown on a turnover-free afternoon by Wentz, who was appointed the backup to Murray ahead of the 2024 first-round draft pick McCarthy for his considerable edge in experience.</p><p>Wentz went helped the Vikings convert eight of 15 third downs and posted a 123.5 passer rating in another memorable comeback among many in five seasons under O'Connell, who has yet to win a playoff game.</p><p>"This one will stick with me for a long time," O'Connell said.</p><p>Momentum shifted when the Packers were stopped on fourth-and-1.</p><p>Love finished 21 for 42 for 387 yards and two first-half touchdowns to Christian Watson, but the two late turnovers and a 3-for-12 conversion rate on third downs loomed large as the Packers picked right up where they left off with a five-game losing streak that ended last season.</p><p>The Packers lost four times after leading in the second half by at least two possessions, including their wild card playoff collapse against the Bears, who outscored the Packers 25-6 in the fourth quarter of that game.</p><p>Green Bay coach Matt LaFleur might have mistakenly triggered this meltdown with his decision to take rookie Trey Smack's field goal off the board to set up a fourth-and-1 on an offside penalty. Love was stuffed at the line with a five-point lead, and the Vikings went the other way for the go-ahead score by Jones, the former Packers favorite who had yet to reach the end zone against his former team.</p><p>The Packers actually four defensive penalties on that drive, starting with a seemingly innocent encroachment call on Jonathan Ford.</p><p>Javon Bullard, whose injurious hit on Murray was flagged, was called for illegal contact to negate a third-down sack. Rookie Chris McClellan was penalized for a late hit on Wentz to wipe out a third-down incompletion. Then Xavier McKinney's defensive holding call erased an end-zone interception by Evan Williams, and Jones scored on the next play.</p><p>Though the penalties on McClellan and McKinney in particular were contested by the Packers, they had only themselves to blame for this collapse.</p><p>"Momentum is a strong thing," Watson said, "and we didn't respond."</p><h3>Injury report</h3><h3></h3><p>Murray seemed to be doing well after the game, O'Connell said, but the timetable for his return was unknown. ... Packers LG Aaron Banks (knee) was inactive, giving Donovan Jennings his first career start.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Packers:</b> at New York Jets on Sept. 20.</p><p><b>Vikings:</b> vs. the Bears at Soldier Field on Sept. 20.<br></p>

entries.title: A year after Operation Midway Blitz, Chicago celebrates 'strength' at the Mexican Independence Day Parade
entries.summary: <p>A year after immigration threats tempered many of Chicago's Mexican Independence Day celebrations, this year's parade aimed to bring back the full 400,000 spectators it expects to garner.</p><p>Last year's parade <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/05/mexican-independence-day-parade-little-village-immigration-ice-threat" target="_blank" >continued as planned</a>, despite fears of immigration raids during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>, President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement campaign targeting Chicago. But, leaders encouraged would-be attendees to do what they felt would be safest and view the parade from home, if they desired.</p><p>This year, the theme of the 55th annual event was "United We Ride: Stronger Than Ever." Held by the Little Village Chamber of Commerce, organizers said the event is one of the largest parades in the Midwest and serves as a cultural celebration and an economic driver for local businesses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f90000" name="image-f90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/44fca55/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F75%2F1df6f08c48e79b7fc74e8d2f1401%2Fmexicandayparade-260914-33-flag.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2192851/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F75%2F1df6f08c48e79b7fc74e8d2f1401%2Fmexicandayparade-260914-33-flag.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c99fca9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F75%2F1df6f08c48e79b7fc74e8d2f1401%2Fmexicandayparade-260914-33-flag.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Participants carry large Mexican flags down 26th Street during the 55th Annual Mexican Independence Day Parade in Chicago's Little Village neighborhood on Sunday, September 13, 2026. entries.summary: <p>A man whose age was not immediately available was in serious condition Sunday after he was shot in the stomach in the South Shore neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>Police said the man had been involved in a verbal argument with an unknown assailant who fired shots along the 2900 block of East 77th Street at about 3:15 p.m.</p><p>The victim was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was initially reported in serious condition, police said.</p><p>Area Two detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Fire fall to Revolution 2-1 at Soldier Field
entries.summary: <p>Dor Turgeman had a first-half goal and a second-half assist, Peyton Miller scored in his 50th MLS start and the New England Revolution beat the Chicago Fire 2-1 on Sunday at Soldier Field.</p><p>New England (13-8-4) moved into sole possession of third place in the Eastern Conference with 43 points, 11 behind first-place Nashville.</p><p>Chicago (11-7-6) was coming off a 1-1 draw against Inter Miami CF in front of a club-record 63,094 fans.</p><p>Turgeman opened the scoring in the 39th minute. He won a one-one-one race with Chicago defender Sam Rogers for a long ball and sent a shot past a diving Chris Brady.</p><p>Miller made it 2-0 lead in the 47th when he was left wide open at the far post to tap in a pass across the goal by Turgeman.</p><p>Maren Haile-Selassie guided in a shot into the far corner from the top of the 18-yard box in the 62nd to pull Chicago within 2-1.</p><p>New England coach Marko Mitrović returned to Chicago to face his former club after serving as an assistant coach with the Fire from 2016-19.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>New England: Hosts Orlando on Saturday.</p><p>Chicago: At Nashville on Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Grandmas go head-to-head over nickname used by child
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My grandson is 2 and has started to call me "Mimi." The problem is that his other grandmother chose Mimi for herself. My daughter-in-law is annoyed and does not want him calling me Mimi. She also doesn't want me to be called Mom-Mom because he calls her Ma-Ma. Am I wrong to be upset? I've been an active caregiver in this child's life since his birth. His other Mimi does not live nearby and makes no effort to be in her grandchild's life — not even by phone. She just uses the term Mimi to sound good to her Facebook friends.</p><p>I know this is silly, but is it wrong for me to be upset? He needs something simple to call me when we go to playgrounds and can't find me. I feel that he can have two Mimis. I grew up with two moms. — <i>NICKNAME IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR NICKNAME:</b> More than one Mimi could be confusing. The most important thing is your relationship with your grandchild, not who has dibs on a certain name. I suggest you let the other grandmother claim "Mimi" while you collaborate with the little boy on a new nickname for you. If he takes part in the decision, it will be easier for him to remember and a lot more special.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been married for 12 years and have two stepchildren. My 37-year-old stepson is the challenging one. He's the biggest cheapskate I have come across in my entire life. Although he earns a good living in his profession, he rarely picks up the tab when we go out to dinner or drinks, and he almost never picks up his own tab, either. He seems to expect that we, as parents, are obligated to take care of his expenses.</p><p>My wife has recently begun picking up his portion, but I find it infuriating that he makes no gesture at all to pay his own way. Should I just let it go and continue letting his mother pick up his portion (from her separate account), while I continue to stress about it? — <i>CHEAPSKATE'S STEPDAD IN NEW MEXICO</i></p><p><b>DEAR STEPDAD:</b> Has your wife asked you not to talk with her son about this? If she hasn't, have you told him he's too old for Mom to constantly pay his tab, particularly in light of the fact that he's a fully employed adult? (One would think he should have volunteered, if only occasionally.) I will assume you have told your wife how you feel about this, that when she picks up her son's portion it makes you lose your appetite. Start there, but if she continues, remember that that money is hers, and how she chooses to spend it is her business.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> The manager of the dining room in my senior living center has a habit of shaking hands with residents at their tables. To avoid his hand, I often say my hand is wet or greasy. How can I best decline his unsanitary effort? — <i>HEALTHY HANDS IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR HEALTHY:</b> The manager wants to appear friendly and welcoming. Because you prefer not to shake hands while dining, simply tell him as much. If you say it with a polite smile and a good-natured tone, it shouldn't cause embarrassment.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: State's attorney's proposed pretrial changes undermine justice
entries.summary: <p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke’s recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountystatesattorney.org/news/icymi-states-attorney-burke-pens-chicago-tribune-op-ed-electronic-monitoring-system-broken" target="_blank" >calls</a> for legislative changes to how pretrial release works — and criticism of the judges making those decisions — is deeply disappointing.</p><p>The presumption of innocence and due process are foundational principles of our legal system, so it is troubling to see O’Neill Burke, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and judge, attacking these concepts and the judiciary's independent decision-making.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/19/23960567/pretrial-fairness-act-illinois-criminal-justice-equity-lisel-petis" >Pretrial Fairness Act</a> requires judges to consider the unique facts of each case and person when deciding whether someone should be detained.</p><p>O’Neill Burke says she supports the law’s removal of the role of money in those decisions, but then suggests that the seriousness of the allegation alone should require detention.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d50000" name="module-d50000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Judges already account for the severity of the allegations when determining pretrial release, and requiring incarceration based on the charge alone would be both unconstitutional and a disaster in a county where 1 out of 3 people charged with a felony is ultimately found not guilty or has their case dismissed.</p><p>Take our client Vanessa Sanders, who was charged with first-degree murder after she stabbed her abusive boyfriend in a clear act of self-defense.</p><p>Citing the prosecution, media initially covered Vanessa as a woman who killed her boyfriend because <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/6/24/18442390/prosecutors-woman-fatally-stabbed-man-for-pulling-her-hair" >“he pulled her hair.”</a> In reality, Sanders had her hair ripped from her scalp before she defended herself.</p><p>Like the vast majority of people facing a murder charge, Vanessa was detained. She spent over seven years in jail awaiting trial at the snail’s pace of the Cook County courts. When finally released on electronic monitoring, Vanessa was present for every court hearing, hoping to clear her name. Earlier this summer, it took a jury one hour to find her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/24/prosecutors-expected-to-offer-new-deal-to-woman-accused-of-killing-boyfriend-as-trial-kicks-off" >not guilty</a>. But a person who is acquitted never gets that time back and never gets restitution for the years of freedom they were denied.</p><p>When the question is asked, “Why are some people charged with serious offenses like murder sometimes released pretrial?” the answer is often that their cases look like Vanessa’s.</p><p>Vanessa should never have been jailed.</p><p>Despite the seriousness of her charge, the fact that Vanessa had a strong self-defense claim and the deceased was an intimate partner with a history of physical abuse shows she was not a danger to the public.</p><p>Clearly, prosecutors don’t always get it right when it comes to charging.</p><p>Giving the state’s attorney the power to effectively determine who gets locked up simply by choosing what charges to file doesn’t just undermine judicial discretion, it risks rigging the system so prosecutors control both the accusation and its consequence.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div O’Neill Burke's blanket policies to seek detention in many cases have caused the jail population to be higher now than before the Pretrial Fairness Act took effect. That’s apparently not enough detention, even though crime rates are at historic lows and have consistently fallen over time, despite an uptick during COVID-19.</p><p>It is also worth noting an area where O’Neill Burke has done almost nothing to hold people who commit violence against the public responsible for their actions: employees of the federal government.</p><p>The sole prosecution O’Neill Burke has undertaken since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/08/how-operation-midway-blitz-played-out" >Operation Midway Blitz</a> is a misdemeanor charge against an off-duty U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/12/ice-adam-saracco-attack-robert-held" >attacked a senior citizen</a> filming him at a gas station — despite the option to charge a felony based on the victim’s age. The state’s reasoning was simply that a misdemeanor was “more appropriate.” In contrast, our clients who are not law enforcement officers are consistently charged with the highest possible offense.</p><p>Notably, O’Neill Burke also didn’t complain about the lack of pretrial detention in that case or demand incarceration for the agent as part of his guilty plea.</p><p>And while the state’s attorney has not acted on the staggering violence ICE has directed at community members responding to the detention of their neighbors for civil immigration violations, she has prosecuted <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/02/26/why-is-the-cook-county-states-attorney-prosecuting-nonviolent-ice-protesters/" target="_blank" >more than 100 people</a> for protesting that violence.</p><p>O’Neill Burke has supported important reforms, but her actions over the last 18 months have raised questions about the consistency of her commitment to fairness in the criminal process. </p><p>The presumption of innocence requires individualized decisions regarding pretrial release, and law enforcement officers deserve to be held to a higher standard — not let off easier than the public.</p><p><i>Sharone R. Mitchell Jr. is the Cook County public defender.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: New report finds 35% of Chicago households don’t have sufficient food
entries.summary: <p>An estimated 35% of households in Chicago face some form of food insecurity, according to a report published Monday by the Greater Chicago Food Depository.</p><p>The depository, which supplies food to hundreds of food pantries across Cook County, partnered for the first time with NORC at the University of Chicago to release “Hunger in Chicago Report,” detailing which communities and types of households face some level of food insecurity, which is defined as experiencing disrupted eating patterns or reduced food.</p><p>Chicago residents who participated in the survey this summer were asked a series of questions, such as if household members in the past 30 days had either skipped meals or reduced portions because there wasn’t enough money to buy food.</p><p>The report released Monday indicates food insecurity is more widespread than what previous reports had indicated. In 2024, about 13% of households in Illinois were experiencing food insecurity and about 24% were marginally food insecure, according to an analysis of data from the <a class="Link" href="https://ukcpr.uky.edu/resources" target="_blank" ><u>University of Kentucky Center for Poverty Research</u></a>.</p><p>Kate Maehr, chief executive officer for the Greater Chicago Food Depository, said the food insecurity people are experiencing is driven by inflation driving up grocery prices and families still recovering from changes to the economy since the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“The data is so stark, and the stakes are so high,” Maehr said. “This is a basic, moral issue. I believe that food is a basic human right, and more than a third of the households in our great city are struggling with access to something as basic as food.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-530000" name="html-embed-module-530000"></a><div style="min-height:306px" id="datawrapper-vis-OtYVx"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/OtYVx/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-OtYVx"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/OtYVx/full.png" alt="Food insecurity by population type (Stacked Bars)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The greater need for food comes amid changes to the largest food assistance program, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. SNAP has undergone <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/30/snap-food-assistance-cutoffs-begin-friday-in-illinois-what-you-need-to-know" target="_blank" ><u>expanded work requirements</u></a> for participants and will dramatically shift program costs to states as part of President Donald Trump’s massive tax and spending plan often referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was signed into law last year.</p><p>Already in Illinois, participation in the federally-funded food assistance program has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/27/illinois-sees-16-drop-in-snap-enrollment-one-year-after-food-program-overhaul" target="_blank" ><u>fallen by 16% compared to 2025</u></a>, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. As of June, the number of people receiving SNAP benefits dropped to nearly 1.6 million people — the lowest number of people receiving food assistance in the state since 2009.</p><p>Maehr described the changes as “the rug being pulled out from under the feet of families that were vulnerable, and it took away this critical resource for so many people.”</p><p>Food insecurity is particularly pronounced on the South Side, where 51% of residents surveyed indicated they either had very low or low food security, according to the report.</p><p>Among the city’s racial groups, Black residents reported the highest level of food insecurity at 61%, according to the depository’s report. In contrast, only 14% of white households reported having limited access to food.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ab0000" name="image-ab0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/36f90c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F6c%2Fdc3ac1c84b2db65c9d4bcdefad08%2Fhungerreport-260914-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7e225c6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F6c%2Fdc3ac1c84b2db65c9d4bcdefad08%2Fhungerreport-260914-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8ec83ea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F6c%2Fdc3ac1c84b2db65c9d4bcdefad08%2Fhungerreport-260914-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Volunteers help pack food in an assembly line-fashion at the Greater Chicago Food Depository’s warehouse in Archer Heights, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. employed in some capacity, and about 27% of food insecure residents were retired, the report found. entries.summary: <p>White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Justin Ishbia’s</u></a> company, Canal Edge LLC, has proposed a mixed-use development called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" ><u>the Railyards as the site for a new White Sox stadium</u></a>, which would be built where an Amtrak railyard now operates.</p><p>The rail company is simultaneously shifting its maintenance operations from the relatively isolated site of the proposed stadium to a 24/7 facility that would stretch into residential areas in Chinatown through Bridgeport.</p><p>In recent months, a coalition has formed to address the environmental and economic impact a Sox stadium move and expanded Amtrak presence would have on Bridgeport and Chinatown.</p><p>Here’s what you need to know.</p><p></p><h3>Why do the White Sox want a new stadium?</h3><p>The team is under lease at the state-owned Rate Field only through 2029, with the option to extend through 2030 before a new lease is signed.</p><h3>Where would the new stadium be located?</h3><p>The stadium would be situated within a parcel of land alongside the Chicago River, stretching from Roosevelt Road to the north to 18th Street to the south, and bordered by the Chicago River on its east side and Canal Street to its west.</p><h3>Who is behind the proposal?</h3><p>Justin Ishbia. He’s a minority owner of the White Sox and co-founder of Shore Capital Partners, the Loop-based private equity firm that has boosted his net worth beyond $4 billion. Shore Capital is behind the Railyards project and is helping to finance Amtrak’s new maintenance facility in Bridgeport. He has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>repeatedly stated interest</u></a> in a new stadium for the Sox.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3d0000" name="image-3d0000"></a> <picture The property is across the Chicago River from where the Chicago Fire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/03/chicago-fire-football-club-breaks-ground-650-million-stadium-78" target="_blank" ><u>broke ground</u></a> earlier this year on its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/17/mayor-brandon-johnson-425m-tif-subsidy-the-78" target="_blank" ><u>$750 million stadium</u></a> at The 78.</p><p>The ballpark itself would be privately financed, a source with direct knowledge of the planning told the Chicago Sun-Times. But there would be an ask for public funding for local infrastructure, including for nearby roads, bridges and potentially a new Metra station, though details haven’t been finalized.</p><h3>What do the White Sox say about all this?</h3><p>The team, which previously said it was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>solely focused</u></a> on the concept of a stadium alongside the Chicago Fire’s stadium at The 78, said last weekend it will evaluate the outcomes of the Railyards site’s environmental and transit studies to decide whether to consider it as a viable option for their next home.</p><p>The White Sox are owned by Jerry Reinsdorf, who remains in control of the team's stadium decisions until he decides to sell the team. He has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-ownership-transfer-new-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>the option</u></a> to sell to Ishbia as soon as 2029.</p><h3>What else is planned beyond a stadium?</h3><p>The mixed-use proposal also would include a Northwestern Medicine “healthcare presence” as well as transit-oriented residential, commercial and retail development. But the concept is in its early stages. A monthslong study on the feasibility of transportation and environmental evaluations is just beginning, the company said in a statement.</p><h3>How is Amtrak involved?</h3><p>As Ishbia looks to take over Amtrak land in the South Loop, his rail company has secured land in Bridgeport and is now looking to start work on building a 24/7 maintenance facility there as soon as this fall with the financing help of one of Ishbia's companies. Operations could start as soon as 2027, Amtrak previously said.</p><p>Amtrak received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://www.doi.gov/oepc/nepa/categorical-exclusions" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the federal government for the project, which allows it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>While the company said it will still conduct “<a class="Link" href="https://mwmaintenancefacility.com/" target="_blank" ><u>standard due-diligence investigations</u></a>,” residents worry the new facility could tank property values, particularly because of the potential for Rate Field being shuttered and the sound, smells or health hazards emanating from the train maintenance facility.</p><p></p><h3>What do elected officials have to say?</h3><p>Eleventh Ward Ald. Nicole Lee, whose ward encompasses Bridgeport and Rate Field, said the Sox's move out and Amtrak’s move in would be “devastating” for the area and called it a “betrayal.”</p><p>Ald. Jason Ervin (28th), whose ward would encompass the new stadium site, said he would have an open mind but would focus on “what’s in the best interests” of his ward and the city. </p><div Even the School of the Art Institute of Chicago is hosting a fall exhibition celebration on Wednesday.</p><p>Pucker said the expanded Exhibition Week is a good opportunity for Chicagoans and those intimidated by the art world to sample the scene, even if they have never visited a gallery. “Being curious is so underrated,” Pucker said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoexhibitionweek.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Exhibition Week</u></b></a></h3><b>When:</b> Through Sept. 20<br><b>Where:</b> Select Chicago galleries<br><b>Tickets:</b> Galleries are free to enter, but some events are ticketed</div> </div><p>If you’re out of town or too busy to experience this year’s Chicago Exhibition Week, fear not: Many participating galleries are keeping the exhibitions that open this week through the fall. Born and raised near the border region around El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, the artist's pop art style is inspired by his everyday life in the Pilsen neighborhood and the South Side of Chicago.</p><p>Classic cars, public housing, tires and other objects are constants throughout Villa’s work, crowning subjects in portraits such as “The Poet.” Keep your eyes peeled for other concept portraits such as “The Butterfly Catcher” and “The Visionary,” which draw on the artist’s experiences in a border town and are meant to be read as poems with multitudes.</p><p>Many of Villa’s works have been shown at the National Museum of Mexican Art in Pilsen, where he once directed the museum’s youth arts program, Yollicalli Arts Reach.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Your guide to fall culture in Chicago </b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f6c56c02-ac5f-11f1-988e-bd5e5ce8e98f"><li>The next big thing is happening on Chicago’s small stages. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/things-to-do/2026/09/04/theater-to-see-chicago-fall-storefront-tickets-new-plays-musicals" target="_blank" ><u>Here are 10 plays and musicals</u></a> not to miss this theater season.</li><li>The ultimate guide to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2026/09/10/chicago-fall-film-festivals-events-things-to-do-movies-ciff-cuff-reeling" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s fall film festivals</u></a>, from Oscar contenders to local standouts</li><li>Evanston’s $32 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>new Northlight Theatre</u></a> wasn’t built for big crowds. It’s built for new plays.</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/08/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism-art-institute-chicago-paintings-impressionist-mural-worlds-fair-1893" target="_blank" ><u>“Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism”</u></a> is the Art Institute’s first deep-dive into Cassatt in more than 25 years and explores some of her historical Chicago ties.</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Ben Johnson (59 points) 'didn't get into this profession trying to be mediocre'
entries.summary: <p>CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Minutes after scoring 59 points, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson wasn’t shy about his goals for his team.</p><p>“We didn't get into this profession trying to be mediocre, average,” he said after Sunday’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/13/bears-panthers-podcast-offense-ben-johnson-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >59-37 win against the Panthers</a>. “That's every NFL team. That is what it is. We make decisions over the course of a week, what's best for our football team to win the game. That's the most important thing, and that goes into everything that we do.”</p><p>The Bears’ 59 points were the third-most in the history of the franchise and the most in 46 years. It was the most Johnson had scored as a play-caller; the 2024 Lions scored 52 twice, once against the Titans and again against the Jaguars.</p><p>The 2022 Bears, by contrast, totaled 52 points over their first three games of the season. The 2023 team had 47. The 2024 team had 53. </p><p>Johnson was asked whether his attitude prompted him to go for it on fourth-and-one from his own 21 in the second quarter. He said it was not, but reiterated what he said during training camp — that the he has high, almost-impossible goals for his team. He wants to surpass the 2013 Broncos, who averaged a league-record 37.9 points per game. He wants to go undefeated. And he wants to win multiple championships.</p><p>Most other coaches in the league want to as well. What makes Johnson different, if anything, is that he says it out loud.</p><p>“We want to be the highest scoring, we want to have the most wins, we want to win Super Bowls,” he said. “We want to. Like, that's what we do.”<br></p>
